stories.title: Exploited Outlook spoofing zero-day CVE-2026-124194 leaks NTLMv2 hashes, added to CISA KEV

writeup.what_happened: Microsoft's November 2026 Patch Tuesday fixed CVE-2026-124194, a spoofing flaw in classic Outlook (CVSS 6.5) that Microsoft says is being exploited in the wild. CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 10 November 2026. Rapid7 reports that opening a specially crafted file makes Outlook silently connect to an attacker-controlled location and leak the user's NTLMv2 hash, which can be cracked or relayed live to services lacking SMB/LDAP signing or Extended Protection. Sources disagree on the release's total size, with counts ranging from about 1,092 to 1,260 fixes.
writeup.why_it_matters: Outlook runs on nearly every Windows endpoint, and leaked NTLMv2 hashes give attackers a path to impersonate users against file servers, LDAP and other internal services. The flaw is confirmed exploited, CISA's federal remediation deadline is 24 November 2026, and public proof-of-concept code is reported to exist, although Rapid7 says there was no public disclosure before release. No EPSS score is available yet. Rapid7 notes the moderate CVSS score understates its value for both mass credential harvesting and targeted intrusions.
affected_versions: All supported versions of classic Outlook (per Rapid7)
fixed_versions: Microsoft November 2026 security updates for Office and Microsoft 365 Apps (released 10 November 2026)
recommended_actions: Deploy the November 2026 Office and Microsoft 365 Apps updates to all classic Outlook installations before 24 November 2026, and confirm update channels have picked up the build.
Block outbound SMB (TCP 445 and 139) from endpoints to the internet at the perimeter and host firewall to stop hash leakage to external hosts.
Add high-value accounts to the Protected Users group and restrict outbound NTLM where possible to blunt captured-hash abuse.
Enforce SMB signing, LDAP signing and channel binding, and Extended Protection for Authentication to reduce NTLM relay risk.
Hunt for Outlook-initiated SMB or WebDAV connections to public addresses, and reset passwords for affected users if any are found.

hunting_steps: Use the vulnerability inventory to list devices still exposed to CVE-2026-124194 and prioritize them for patching.
Search network telemetry for outlook.exe connecting to public IPs on TCP 445 or 139 since late October 2026, and note the user and remote address.
For each hit, review emails and attachments the user received shortly before the connection to identify the lure and other recipients.
Check identity logs for NTLM authentications by affected accounts from unfamiliar devices or IPs, which may indicate relay or cracked-hash use.
Reset credentials for confirmed affected users and block the identified external hosts at the perimeter.

stories.title: CISA adds chained Barracuda ESG auth bypass and root command injection flaws to KEV

writeup.what_happened: On 10 November 2026, CISA added two Barracuda Networks flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. CVE-2026-116606 (CVSS 9.3) is an authentication bypass in Email Security Gateway (ESG). It lets an unauthenticated remote attacker call a configuration-import function and restore a crafted backup archive, which changes the appliance's global configuration. CVE-2026-111560 (CVSS 8.6) is an OS command injection in a timezone value that runs commands as root; CISA says it affects ESG plus Load Balancer, ADC, Message Archiver, WAF Control Center, WAF and Web Security Gateway, and that the two flaws can be chained.
writeup.why_it_matters: CISA lists both flaws as exploited in the wild, and chained together they could plausibly let an unauthenticated attacker run root commands on an internet-facing mail gateway that sees all inbound mail. Public proof-of-concept code is reported for the authentication bypass (EPSS 1.6%; 1.1% for the command injection). The KEV remediation due date is 13 November 2026, only three days after the listing.
affected_versions: Barracuda Email Security Gateway (ESG): CVE-2026-116606 and CVE-2026-111560, versions not stated

Barracuda Load Balancer, Application Delivery Controller (ADC), Message Archiver (BMA), WAF Control Center (WCC), Web Application Firewall (WAF), Web Security Gateway (WSG): CVE-2026-111560, versions…
recommended_actions: Apply Barracuda's mitigations and updates for both CVEs on all ESG and other affected Barracuda appliances before the 13 November 2026 KEV deadline, or take exposed appliances offline if no mitigation is available.
Restrict the ESG administrative interface so it is not reachable from the internet, allowing only trusted management networks.

Review ESG configuration, admin accounts, timezone settings and configuration-import or restore history for changes you cannot explain, and follow CISA's forensics triage guidance on any appliance that was exposed.

Treat any appliance showing tampering as compromised: rebuild or replace it, and rotate credentials and keys stored on or passing through it, including LDAP and SMTP relay credentials and admin passwords.
Check outbound traffic from the appliance's IP for unusual destinations, and review mail-flow and routing rules for unauthorized changes.

hunting_steps: Inventory all Barracuda ESG, BMA, WAF, WCC, WSG, Load Balancer and ADC appliances and identify which have internet-reachable management interfaces.
Confirm each appliance's patch or mitigation status against Barracuda's advisory.
Pull appliance admin and audit logs and look for configuration import or backup restore events that no administrator initiated, and for unexpected timezone changes.
In firewall or Sentinel network logs, look for outbound connections from appliance IPs to unfamiliar external hosts, which may indicate post-exploitation activity.
Check Defender vulnerability management for any Barracuda assets it tracks with these CVEs.

stories.title: Huntress details four evolving ClickFix attack chains, including lateral movement and PNG-hidden payloads

writeup.what_happened: Huntress reports that ClickFix, a social engineering technique that tricks users into pasting and running attacker-supplied commands, has evolved. According to Huntress, recent chains add lateral movement, payloads hidden inside PNG image files, Node.js-based remote access trojans, and a browser cache abuse technique. The available summary does not give indicators, specific malware families, or victim details.
writeup.why_it_matters: ClickFix gets around many email and download controls because the user runs the command themselves, usually through the Windows Run dialog or a terminal, so any Windows endpoint with a human user is exposed. Huntress says the activity now goes beyond a single host to lateral movement, which raises the impact of one successful lure. No CVE or patch applies, so detection and user controls are the main defenses.
recommended_actions: Hunt for Run dialog (RunMRU) entries and explorer.exe-spawned shells that contain PowerShell, mshta, curl or encoded commands, and investigate any hits.
Hunt for node.exe running from user-writable paths such as AppData or Temp and making outbound connections, which may indicate a Node.js RAT.

Where business needs allow, restrict the Win+R Run dialog for standard users through Group Policy and enable Attack Surface Reduction rules that block obfuscated scripts and Office or script child processes.
After any confirmed ClickFix execution, check for lateral movement from the affected host and rotate the user's credentials.
Brief users that legitimate sites never ask them to paste commands into Run, PowerShell or a terminal to fix errors or pass CAPTCHA checks.

title: Suspicious Command Entered in Windows Run Dialog (ClickFix)
id: 6087785c-4d91-5d4a-abd2-15842af17c21
status: experimental
description: Detects Run dialog history (RunMRU) entries containing script interpreters or download utilities, which matches ClickFix lures that get users to paste and run malicious commands. Huntress reports this tradecraft is evolving and in active use. AI-generated, untested.

  category: registry_set
detection:
  selection_key:
    TargetObject|contains: \Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\RunMRU\
  selection_tools:
    Details|contains:
    - powershell
    - pwsh

selection_tools alternative 2, contained text at the end
selection_tools alternative 3, contained text at the end

elastic.label: Elastic (Lucene, ECS)
elastic.query: registry.path:*\\Software\\Microsoft\\Windows\\CurrentVersion\\Explorer\\RunMRU\\* AND (winlog.event_data.Details:(*powershell* OR *pwsh* OR *mshta* OR *curl* OR *wget* OR *bitsadmin* OR *certutil* OR *rundll32* OR *regsvr32* OR *msiexec* OR *cmd\ \/c* OR *cmd.exe\ \/c* OR *conhost*)) AND (NOT registry.path:*\\MRUList)

hunting_steps: Query RunMRU registry writes over the last 30 days for entries with interpreters, download tools, URLs or encoded content.
Correlate hits with process creation where explorer.exe is the parent of powershell, mshta, cmd or curl, and look at the command lines.
Look for follow-on activity on affected hosts: network connections to newly seen domains, image files written then read by script hosts, and node.exe running from user profile paths.
For confirmed hosts, check remote logons, SMB, WMI or WinRM activity to other devices to scope lateral movement.
Review browser history around the execution time to find the lure site and block it.

hunting_queries.title: ClickFix-style commands written to RunMRU
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceRegistryEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RegistryKey has @"Explorer\RunMRU" and RegistryValueName != "MRUList" | where RegistryValueData has_any ("powershell", "pwsh", "mshta", "curl", "certutil", "bitsadmin", "rundll32", "regsvr32", "msiexec", "http") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData | order by Timestamp desc

hunting_queries.title: Explorer-spawned script interpreters with network or encoded commands
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceProcessEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe" | where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "mshta.exe", "cmd.exe", "curl.exe") | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http", "-enc", "-e ", "iex", "invoke-expression", "downloadstring", "-w hidden", "hidden") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine | order by Timestamp desc

hunting_queries.title: Node.js running from user-writable paths with outbound connections
hunting_queries.kql: DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "node.exe" | where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\") | where RemoteIPType == "Public" | summarize Connections = count(), RemoteUrls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 20), RemoteIPs = make_set(RemoteIP, 20) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine | order by Connections desc

stories.title: Railway says attackers stole customer secrets, generating about $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage

writeup.what_happened: BleepingComputer reports that cloud hosting provider Railway says attackers exploited vulnerabilities in its infrastructure and stole customer authentication secrets. According to Railway, the stolen secrets were used to run up roughly $740,000 in fraudulent AI usage. Credentials for as many as 100,000 workspaces may have been exposed. The sources do not name the vulnerabilities, the timeline, or which secret types were taken.
writeup.why_it_matters: Railway confirms the stolen secrets were abused. Any API keys, cloud credentials, database passwords or Entra ID app secrets stored as Railway environment variables should be treated as compromised. AI provider keys are the confirmed target, but the same secrets may give access to Microsoft 365, Azure or other SaaS tenants your teams connected to Railway-hosted apps.
recommended_actions: Identify every team and project that uses Railway, including shadow IT and developer side projects.
Rotate all secrets stored in Railway workspaces: AI provider API keys, cloud access keys, database credentials, OAuth tokens and Entra ID application client secrets or certificates.
Review billing and usage logs for AI services (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Anthropic and others) for unexplained spikes, and set spending caps and alerts.
Review sign-ins for Entra ID service principals whose credentials were stored in Railway, looking for unfamiliar IP addresses or unusual resource access.
Follow Railway's official notifications for any indicators or detail on the exploited vulnerabilities.

sources.title: Railway breach leads to $740,000 in fraudulent AI charges

hunting_steps: Inventory Railway usage by finding endpoints where the Railway CLI has been run, then contact those owners.
List the secrets each Railway project held and map them to the services they unlock (AI providers, Azure, M365, databases).
For Entra ID applications whose secrets lived in Railway, review service principal sign-ins and audit logs for unfamiliar source IPs or new activity after the suspected exposure window.
Check AI provider and Azure OpenAI usage and billing for anomalous consumption.
Confirm that every exposed credential has been rotated and the old one revoked, not just replaced.

hunting_queries.title: Endpoints running the Railway CLI (inventory of Railway users)
hunting_queries.kql:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("railway", "railway.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("railway login", "railway up", "railway variables", "@railway/cli")
| summarize Executions = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, AccountName
| order by LastSeen desc

hunting_queries.title: Cloud app activity by OAuth or service apps from new IP addresses
hunting_queries.kql:
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where isnotempty(IPAddress) and isnotempty(ApplicationId)
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Actions = count() by Application, ApplicationId, IPAddress, CountryCode
| where FirstSeen > ago(14d)
| order by Actions desc

stories.title: Compromised Qubole AWS IAM credentials used to steal data from multiple customer AWS environments

writeup.what_happened: BleepingComputer reported on 10 November 2026 that a threat actor obtained IAM credentials tied to the AWS account of Qubole, a big data platform. According to the report, the attacker used that trusted access to reach the AWS environments of several Qubole customers and exfiltrate data from them. The available reporting does not name the affected customers, explain how the credentials were compromised, or list indicators of compromise.
writeup.why_it_matters: Third-party SaaS platforms such as Qubole usually get cross-account IAM roles or access keys with broad read access to customer S3 data. Abuse of that access looks like normal vendor activity unless it is baselined. Exploitation is confirmed, so any organization that has granted Qubole access to its AWS accounts should treat its environment as potentially exposed until it has reviewed the logs.
affected_versions: Organizations that granted Qubole IAM access (cross-account roles or access keys) to their AWS environments
recommended_actions: Inventory every IAM role, trust policy and access key that grants Qubole or other third-party platforms access to your AWS accounts. Revoke or suspend that access if it is not actively needed.
Rotate any access keys shared with Qubole. Require a unique external ID on cross-account roles and restrict them to known source IP ranges where the vendor supports it.

Review CloudTrail for AssumeRole calls and data-access events by vendor roles during the past months. Look for unusual source IPs, new regions, bulk S3 GetObject or ListBucket activity, and large egress.
Reduce vendor role permissions to the specific buckets and actions the integration needs, and turn on S3 data events and GuardDuty for exfiltration anomalies.
Contact Qubole for confirmation of whether your tenant was affected and for any indicators they can share.

sources.title: Hackers exploit trusted AWS access to breach multiple cloud environments

hunting_steps: List all IAM roles whose trust policy references Qubole or another external vendor account, and record the role ARNs.
If AWS is connected to Defender for Cloud Apps, search CloudAppEvents for AssumeRole activity by those roles. Otherwise search CloudTrail directly in Sentinel.
Baseline the source IPs, user agents and regions normally used by the vendor role. Flag sessions that fall outside that baseline.
For suspicious sessions, pivot to S3 data events (GetObject, ListObjects, ListBuckets) and measure volume per session to spot bulk exfiltration.
Check for persistence created by the vendor role, such as CreateAccessKey, CreateUser, PutBucketPolicy or changes to role trust policies.

hunting_queries.title: AWS activity referencing Qubole roles or principals
hunting_queries.kql: CloudAppEvents | where Timestamp > ago(90d) | where Application == "Amazon Web Services" | where tostring(RawEventData) has "qubole" | summarize Events = count(), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 50), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountDisplayName, ActionType | order by Events desc

hunting_queries.title: AssumeRole and S3 data access volume per principal and source IP
hunting_queries.kql: CloudAppEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where Application == "Amazon Web Services" | where ActionType in ("AssumeRole", "GetObject", "ListBuckets", "ListObjects", "ListObjectsV2") | summarize Events = count(), Actions = make_set(ActionType, 10) by AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, CountryCode | order by Events desc

hunting_queries.title: Persistence or policy changes made in AWS
hunting_queries.kql: CloudAppEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where Application == "Amazon Web Services" | where ActionType in ("CreateAccessKey", "CreateUser", "UpdateAssumeRolePolicy", "PutBucketPolicy", "AttachRolePolicy", "PutRolePolicy") | project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, ActionType, IPAddress, CountryCode, ObjectName | order by Timestamp desc

stories.title: Microsoft November 2026 updates fix dozens of Office, Excel, Outlook and SharePoint flaws

writeup.what_happened: Microsoft's Security Update Guide lists a large batch of Office-family vulnerabilities fixed on 10 November 2026, most of them remote code execution bugs in Excel (heap and stack overflows, use-after-free, double free), plus RCE flaws in PowerPoint, Access, Outlook and Office itself. On SharePoint, Microsoft fixed two deserialization RCE flaws that require an authenticated attacker (CVE-2026-120000, CVE-2026-109464), a cross-site scripting spoofing bug, and an incorrect-authorization privilege escalation flaw (CVE-2026-120002) that NVD scores CVSS 9.9. The release also includes two network-exploitable Outlook heap overflows (CVE-2026-119995, CVE-2026-119996), a local Outlook RCE, an Office security feature bypass where the UI fails to warn of unsafe actions (CVE-2026-119998), and several information disclosure bugs. The sources do not list affected build numbers, and neither Microsoft nor CISA reports exploitation or public proof-of-concept code.
writeup.why_it_matters: Office and Outlook run on nearly every Windows endpoint, and malicious documents and email remain a primary initial access route, so this volume of document-parsing RCE bugs widens the phishing attack surface until clients are updated. On-premises SharePoint servers face an authenticated privilege escalation rated CVSS 9.9 and authenticated deserialization RCE, which matter most where SharePoint is internet-facing or broadly accessible to users. None of the CVEs are in CISA KEV, no EPSS scores are available yet, and no exploitation is known, so this is a standard but broad patch priority with SharePoint first.
fixed_versions: Microsoft security updates released 10 November 2026 (build numbers not stated in the sources)
recommended_actions: Apply the November 2026 SharePoint Server updates first, prioritizing internet-facing or widely accessible farms, given the CVSS 9.9 elevation of privilege flaw CVE-2026-120002 and the deserialization RCE flaws.
Push the November 2026 Office, Microsoft 365 Apps, Outlook and Access updates to all endpoints and confirm update channel compliance in Defender Vulnerability Management.
Enforce Attack Surface Reduction rules that block Office applications from creating child processes and from injecting into other processes.
Keep Protected View and Mark-of-the-Web handling enabled for documents from the internet and email, given the Office security feature bypass CVE-2026-119998.
Hunt for Office applications and SharePoint IIS worker processes spawning shells or script interpreters until patching is complete.

stories.title: Microsoft November 2026 Patch Tuesday fixes Windows RCE and privilege escalation flaws

writeup.what_happened: On 10 November 2026 Microsoft released its November Patch Tuesday updates, shipped as cumulative updates for Windows 11 26H2, 25H2, 24H2 and 23H2 and as extended security update KB5131096 for Windows 10, according to BleepingComputer. Microsoft and NVD describe remote code execution flaws in Windows DNS, Windows Shell, Storage Spaces Controller, Active Directory and the Remote Desktop Gateway Service. They also list a network-reachable Print Spooler privilege escalation (CVSS 8.8), local privilege escalation in Win32K, NTFS and the DWM Core Library, and information disclosure in Windows Shell and the iSCSI Target Service. None of the sources report exploitation in the wild or public proof-of-concept code.
writeup.why_it_matters: These components run across most Windows estates. The DNS, Active Directory, Print Spooler and RD Gateway flaws affect high-value servers that attackers often target soon after patches are reverse-engineered. None of the CVEs is in CISA KEV and no EPSS scores are available yet, so this is routine but broad patching, with servers prioritized.
fixed_versions: Windows 11 cumulative updates KB5132061 and KB5131087 (the sources do not map each KB to a version)
recommended_actions: Patch domain controllers, Windows DNS servers, Remote Desktop Gateway hosts and print servers first with the November 2026 cumulative updates.
Deploy KB5132061 or KB5131087 to Windows 11 devices and KB5131096 to Windows 10 ESU devices through your normal update rings.
Disable the Print Spooler service on servers that do not need printing, especially domain controllers.
Limit internet exposure of Remote Desktop and RD Gateway, and require MFA in front of remote access.
Confirm patch coverage with Defender Vulnerability Management and follow up on devices still exposed to the listed CVEs.

stories.title: Nitori discloses network intrusion with possible theft of 37.62 million customer records

writeup.what_happened: Japanese furniture and home goods retailer Nitori says an attacker gained access to a system on its network and may have stolen about 37.62 million customer records, according to BleepingComputer. The sources do not say how the attacker got in, which system was reached, what data fields the records contain, or when the intrusion took place. No threat actor has been named.
writeup.why_it_matters: No vulnerability, product or attacker technique has been disclosed, so there is nothing specific to hunt for in Windows, M365 or edge telemetry. The main risk to most organizations is secondary: phishing and credential-stuffing campaigns that reuse the leaked customer data, especially aimed at staff or customers with ties to Japanese retail.
recommended_actions: Watch for further disclosures from Nitori on the initial access vector and the exposed data types, and reassess if a product vulnerability or attacker tooling is named.
If your organization has a business relationship with Nitori, review data-sharing agreements and confirm which of your data could be in scope.
Brief users and helpdesk staff on likely phishing lures that pose as Nitori or reference recent Nitori purchases.

stories.title: Microsoft's November 2026 updates fix a large batch of Windows elevation of privilege flaws

writeup.what_happened: Microsoft's Security Update Guide published fixes on 10 November 2026 for a large set of Windows elevation of privilege vulnerabilities. They span the kernel, Win32k, the graphics kernel, Desktop Window Manager, Print Spooler components, Windows Installer, Hyper-V, SMB Client, WMI, and a long run of Advanced Rasterization Platform bugs. Most require an attacker who is already authenticated locally. A smaller group is described as network-reachable: Microsoft lists Kerberos (CVE-2026-85844), a Print Spooler path traversal (CVE-2026-112762), NetBIOS (CVE-2026-105551) and File Server Resource Management (CVE-2026-108421) as exploitable by an unauthorized attacker over a network, and the DHCP Client (CVE-2026-113863) over an adjacent network.
writeup.why_it_matters: Local privilege escalation is the step that turns a phished user or a foothold from a stolen session into SYSTEM, credential theft and EDR tampering, and these flaws affect every Windows fleet. No exploitation, KEV listing or public proof-of-concept is reported, and the few scored CVEs sit at CVSS 7.0 to 7.8 with no EPSS data yet. The network-reachable Kerberos, Active Directory Domain Services (CVE-2026-118735, CVE-2026-123387), Print Spooler, NetBIOS and DNS issues deserve priority on domain controllers and servers.
recommended_actions: Deploy the November 2026 cumulative updates to domain controllers first. Kerberos (CVE-2026-85844) and Active Directory Domain Services (CVE-2026-118735, CVE-2026-123387) are network-reachable.

Next, patch servers exposed to the network-reachable flaws: Print Spooler (CVE-2026-112762), NetBIOS (CVE-2026-105551), File Server Resource Management (CVE-2026-108421), DNS (CVE-2026-105520) and Event Collector (CVE-2026-112793).
Disable the Print Spooler service on domain controllers and on servers that do not need printing.
Roll the updates to all workstations and Hyper-V hosts in the normal cycle, then confirm coverage with Defender Vulnerability Management.
Hunt for SYSTEM-level shells spawned from Print Spooler or Windows Installer, a common outcome of local privilege escalation.

stories.title: Microsoft November 2026 Windows updates fix dozens of information disclosure and DoS flaws

writeup.what_happened: On 10 November 2026, Microsoft's Security Update Guide published fixes for 66 Windows CVEs. Most are local information disclosure bugs. The rest are denial of service, security feature bypass, tampering and spoofing issues in components including DNS Server, LSASS, Security Account Manager, Active Directory, DHCP Server, Windows Deployment Services, SSTP, QUIC, Message Queuing, Print Spooler and PowerShell. Microsoft does not report any of these as exploited, and none are in CISA KEV. The scores that are available are moderate, with the highest at CVSS 6.5 for the WLAN Service DoS (CVE-2026-96086).
writeup.why_it_matters: Several flaws can be triggered over the network without authentication, which puts infrastructure servers in scope. They include DNS Server DoS (CVE-2026-96975), DNS information disclosure (CVE-2026-105579), SAM DoS (CVE-2026-112966), SSTP DoS (CVE-2026-105561), QUIC DoS (CVE-2026-105512), Message Queuing DoS (CVE-2026-105515), RMCAST DoS (CVE-2026-116697), DHCP Server spoofing and disclosure (CVE-2026-113773, CVE-2026-105557), WDS path traversal (CVE-2026-118213) and a PowerShell XML external entity disclosure (CVE-2026-122985). Authenticated network DoS bugs in LSASS (CVE-2026-112807) and Active Directory (CVE-2026-105568, CVE-2026-105559) could disrupt domain controllers. There is no known exploitation or public proof of concept, so normal patch cadence is reasonable, with domain controllers, DNS, DHCP, WDS and RRAS/SSTP servers first.
fixed_versions: Microsoft November 2026 security updates released 10 November 2026
recommended_actions: Deploy the November 2026 Windows cumulative updates to domain controllers and to DNS, DHCP, WDS, RRAS/SSTP and Message Queuing servers first.
Confirm that no DNS Server, Message Queuing, WDS or SSTP endpoint is reachable from the internet unless required, and restrict exposed ones at the edge firewall.
Disable unused roles and services such as Message Queuing, Remote Registry, WDS and RMCAST/PGM on servers that do not need them.
Roll the updates out to all remaining Windows endpoints within the standard patch window.
Use Defender Vulnerability Management to verify coverage and chase devices still missing the update.

explainer.concept: NTLM hash leakage and relay: how a file can hand over a user's credentials
explainer.dek: NTLM hash leakage happens when Windows is made to authenticate automatically to an attacker's server, exposing a challenge-response that can be cracked offline or relayed live to another service as that user.
explainer.why_today: The exploited Outlook zero-day in today's lead story works by making Outlook silently connect to an attacker-controlled location and send the user's NTLMv2 response. Whether that becomes a cracked password or a relayed login depends on controls most environments have only partly deployed.

parts.heading: How the leak works
paragraphs: NTLM is a challenge-response protocol. When a Windows client connects to a server that asks for NTLM, the client proves it knows the user's password hash by answering a server-chosen challenge, without sending the password itself. Windows will often do this automatically and silently for resources it treats as reachable, such as a UNC path over SMB or a WebDAV location over HTTP.

Coerced-authentication bugs abuse this. A crafted email, document or file contains a reference to a remote path the attacker controls. When the client processes it, Windows reaches out and performs the NTLM handshake with the attacker's server, which records the NTLMv2 response. No code runs on the victim and no prompt appears, so a medium-severity spoofing or information disclosure label can understate the risk.

parts.heading: Cracking versus relaying
paragraphs: The captured NTLMv2 response can be attacked offline: the attacker guesses passwords and checks each guess against the response. Strong, long passwords make this impractical, while weak or reused ones fall quickly. Machine accounts and managed service accounts with long random passwords are effectively uncrackable this way.

Relaying is the more dangerous outcome because password strength does not matter. The attacker forwards the victim's handshake in real time to a different server, such as a file server, LDAP on a domain controller, AD CS web enrollment or another HTTP service, and is authenticated there as the victim. Relay succeeds only where the target does not bind the authentication to the session: SMB without required signing, LDAP without signing or channel binding, and HTTP services without Extended Protection for Authentication.

parts.heading: What it looks like in telemetry
paragraphs: The leak itself is an outbound connection from a user process to an unusual destination. In Defender XDR, look in DeviceNetworkEvents for Outlook or other Office processes connecting to TCP 445 or to HTTP/WebDAV on public IP addresses, and in DeviceProcessEvents or service events for the WebClient service starting unexpectedly. On endpoints with NTLM outbound auditing enabled, the Microsoft-Windows-NTLM/Operational log records outgoing NTLM authentication attempts with the target server name.

A successful relay shows up on the target: a network logon (event 4624, logon type 3) using NTLM for a user, arriving from an IP address that is not that user's workstation, often followed by LDAP changes, certificate requests or file access the user would not normally perform. Defender for Identity has detections for suspected NTLM relay and NTLM authentication anomalies against domain controllers.

parts.heading: How to shut it down
paragraphs: Patch the coercion bug first, but treat the class as permanent: new coercion paths appear regularly. The durable fix is to make leaked handshakes useless. Block outbound SMB to the internet at the perimeter and on host firewalls, require SMB signing on servers and clients, enforce LDAP signing and channel binding on domain controllers, and enable Extended Protection on IIS, Exchange and AD CS web endpoints. Defaults differ by Windows and Exchange version, so verify the effective setting rather than assuming it.

Reduce NTLM use itself. Put privileged accounts in the Protected Users group, which prevents them from using NTLM, and use the Restrict NTLM group policies in audit mode first to find what still depends on NTLM before blocking outgoing NTLM to remote servers.

takeaways: Deploy the November 2026 Outlook update for the exploited spoofing flaw and confirm coverage of classic Outlook installs, since it is in CISA KEV.

Hunt in DeviceNetworkEvents for OUTLOOK.EXE and other Office processes connecting to public IPs on port 445 or over WebDAV, and confirm outbound SMB to the internet is blocked at the edge and on host firewalls.
Verify SMB signing is required on file servers and domain controllers, and that LDAP signing and channel binding are enforced on every domain controller.
Enable Extended Protection for Authentication on Exchange, AD CS web enrollment and other internal IIS services that accept Windows authentication.
Add admin and other high-value accounts to Protected Users, and turn on NTLM outbound auditing to inventory remaining NTLM dependencies before restricting it.

good_news.headline: Microsoft Research publishes method for detecting backdoored 'sleeper agent' AI models
good_news.summary: The Microsoft Security Blog reports that Microsoft Research has released threat research showing a capable agent model can be turned into a sleeper agent by editing fewer than 10 neurons, passing evaluations but running an attacker's command when a trigger string appears. The work focuses on detecting such tampering, framing model weight integrity as a security concern for both third-party and internally developed models used by unattended, privileged agents.

good_news.summary: Microsoft's Security Update Guide lists November 2026 fixes for heap-based buffer overflows in SQL Server that allow an authorized attacker to execute code or elevate privileges over a network. It also lists two heap overflows in the Microsoft WDAC OLE DB provider for SQL that allow an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network. No exploitation is reported for these flaws.
